title: bandwidth fairness and host smoothing exploratory notes
body:
Summary:

This doc captures exploratory experiments and early hypotheses around inter-GPU bandwidth fairness and host-side transfer smoothing for large-sequence LLM inference. We observed persistent p99 tail spikes that correlate with synchronized large host->GPU transfers (cold KV cache warms, large weight paging) and short-term NVLink/PCIe congestion when many replicas issue heavy reads concurrently. The goal is to prototype mitigations that reduce tail latency without a large throughput penalty and that are compatible with Dedicated clusters and Private deployments.

Key observations (empirical):
- Workload: batched chat (mean seq 512, hot cache) vs long-sequence generation (seq 2k+ with cache miss warmups).
- Hardware: DGX-A100-like nodes (8x A100), mixed NVLink/PCIe fabrics across racks (some hosts have NVLink islands). Tests also run on single-host PCIe-Gen4 machines used in Private.
- Tools used: nsight-sys (nsys) traces, perf + softirq counters, nvprof/NVML sample counters for NVLink, eBPF-based host read tracing, and nccl-tests for synthetic baselines.
- Symptom: 200–400 ms p99 tail spikes on long-seq requests that are otherwise <120 ms p50. Spikes align to periodic bursts of PCIe read latency and NVLink utilization hitting 85–100% for short windows.
- Correlation: When we aligned traces across replicas, the heavy transfers are synchronized — KV cache misses and host-staged weight reads are kicked off nearly simultaneously across many replicas. This leads to transient link saturation and increased NCCL allreduce latency in pipelined scenarios.

Hypotheses:
1) Synchronized host-to-device read bursts create momentary link saturation that magnifies synchronized NCCL collective latency (rings/trees stall waiting for data).
2) Host IO scheduling and naive prefetching strategies are too aggressive — warming too many large pages at once rather than staggered waves.
3) Small changes to request slicing and a lightweight host-side pacing agent can significantly reduce tail without sacrificing steady-state throughput.

Experiment matrix (summary):
- Baseline: current request demux, aggressive prefetch (prefetch whole KV shard), no pacing.
- Variant A: staggered prefetches with fixed jitter window (0-20 ms jitter per replica start).
- Variant B: host-transfer-smoothing daemon (HTS) that enforces per-link inflight byte cap + windowed stripe alignment.
- Variant C: intra-node fairness via token-bucket on NVLink per-replica (soft limit) + HTS.
- Variant D: conservative prefetch (only 2MB ahead) + request slicing into 256-token micro-ops.

What we measured: p50/p90/p99 generation latency, throughput (tokens/sec), NVLink utilization percentiles (10/50/90/99), PCIe read latency distribution, NCCL op times (allreduce, broadcast), CPU softirq and memcpy bandwidth.

Representative results (long-seq scenario, 16-replica mix, synthetic):
- Baseline: p50 110 ms, p90 180 ms, p99 420 ms; tokens/sec 12k; NVLink 99th percentile bursts to 98% utilization; PCIe read tail 12–18 ms.
- Variant A (jitter): p50 115 ms, p90 170 ms, p99 300 ms; tokens/sec 11.6k (3.3% drop).
- Variant B (HTS): p50 120 ms, p90 175 ms, p99 140 ms; tokens/sec 10.9k (9.2% drop).
- Variant C (fairness + HTS): p50 125 ms, p90 160 ms, p99 130 ms; tokens/sec 10.3k (14% drop).
- Variant D (slice conservative): p50 135 ms, p90 215 ms, p99 160 ms; tokens/sec 9.7k (19% drop).

Interpretation:
- Simple jitter reduces worst-case alignment but is brittle for larger clusters — as cluster size grows alignment probability increases and jitter windows must be large, hurting throughput.
- HTS that enforces a sliding inflight-bytes window (we used 32 MB per GPU link as a starting heuristic) smooths out bursts and reduces p99 dramatically while retaining most throughput. The tradeoff is slightly higher p50 due to additional pacing.
- Adding a lightweight fairness layer across replicas (token-bucket where tokens represent allowed NIC/PCIe bytes per time window) helps prevent a single tenant or route from monopolizing transient link capacity; this further tightens tails but increases latency overhead and lowers tokens/sec.
- Aggressive slicing (Variant D) avoided big host reads but introduced overheads in CPU and NCCL op counts — causing throughput regression and some p90 worsening. This suggests slicing should be combined with HTS rather than alone.

Prototype: host-transfer-smoothing daemon (HTS) notes:
- Location: runs on the host agent (sidecar-like) with visibility into in-flight DMA/PCIe ops. For Private deployments, HTS is optional but default-enabled for Dedicated.
- Input signals: queue depth, cumulative in-flight bytes to each GPU, NVML counters, a light eBPF trace for host read start/complete, per-replica request priorities (from runtime). Optionally consumes KV-cache miss hints from the runtime.
- Control knobs: per-link inflight bytes cap, window size (ms), max burst allowance, per-replica priority bias, prefetch concurrency cap.
- Policy: when inflight-bytes > threshold, HTS delays further host staging requests from lower-priority replicas in FIFO order with exponential backoff. For cache warmup, HTS enforces staggered warmup across replicas.
- Implementation sketch: userspace daemon hooks into host staging layer via a small shim (libhoststage) that returns immediately but registers the transfer with HTS; HTS issues the actual DMA read in controlled bursts. Shim fallback for clients ignoring shim: kernel-level cgroups traffic shaping on PCIe is not available, so shim is needed for reliable control.

Microbench commands and trace examples (notes for reproducibility):
- NVLink sampling: nv-nsight or NVML poll every 5ms: nvmlDeviceGetPcieThroughput (read counters) + nvmlDeviceGetFabricStats for NVLink.
- PCIe read latency sampling: eBPF script tracing host->GPU read syscalls and measuring completion times (attached in a separate gists folder).
- NCCL profiling: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and collect timings per-operation; synthetic: nccl-tests allreduce --minbytes 1 --maxbytes 64MB --iter 1000.
- Example ad-hoc: sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:nvme_read_complete { @t[tid] = nsecs; } kretprobe:nvme_io_submit { printf("submit %d\n", pid); }' (we used a specialized program to target our staging path not NVMe).

Edge cases and failure modes observed: 
- HTS interacts poorly with very short lived workloads where the pacing overhead dominates (e.g., seq 32). We should gate HTS by predicted sequence length or in-flight expected bytes.
- On hosts with heterogeneous NVLink islands (partial connectivity), our per-link cap needed to be per-island rather than per-GPU. If not, HTS may over-constrain some paths.
- In private air-gapped setups with older PCIe gen, the inflight cap must be lower; default 32 MB was too high for PCIe Gen3 single root complex. Make adaptive calibration step at startup (micro-benchmark that measures max sustainable read BW and sets threshold).

Open questions / next experiments: 
- Auto-calibration: can we do a micro-benchmark at startup to compute safe inflight-bytes threshold per-link and update HTS dynamically?
- Scheduler integration: should the global scheduler stagger query assignment times to reduce alignment, or is HTS sufficient at the host level? Likely both — scheduler-level coarse staggering + host HTS for fine-grain smoothing.
- KV-cache prefetch policies: can the runtime provide better miss hints (per-token hotness predictions) so HTS does not need to be conservative for all warmups?
- Cloud/AZ-aware policies: multiple replicas spread across zones will have different interconnect characteristics; HTS needs to be region-aware.

Immediate next steps (action items):
- Marco: implement a minimal HTS prototype (shim + daemon) that enforces inflight-bytes cap. Target: PoC in kube cluster with 4 replicas by 2024-11-15.
- Leah: prepare a micro-benchmark script to auto-calibrate per-link thresholds and publish a draft algorithm by 2024-11-08.
- Julian: run cluster-scale trials (16–64 replicas) with Variants A–D and collect p50/p90/p99 + NVLink/PCIe traces by 2024-11-22.
- Aisha: write a short proposal for scheduler-level staggered assignment and its API (how to signal backpressure from HTS) by 2024-11-05.

Notes for reviewers: this is exploratory. The HTS approach is promising for long-sequence, cache-miss heavy workloads (the ones that drive worst tails in our hosted API logs). Be mindful that tradeoffs are workload-dependent. For PLG-hosted customers that care about raw throughput more than tail, we should make HTS configurable and off by default for self-serve clusters; for Dedicated/Enterprise we should enable with conservative defaults and provide tuning knobs in Console.

Appendix (short trace excerpt):
- Timeline sample (aligned across replicas):
  t=0ms: 16 replicas receive generation requests (seq 2048)
  t=2ms: runtime issues KV shard prefetch for each replica (size 6MB)
  t=6–12ms: host starts issuing DMA reads for 16 replicas nearly simultaneously -> NVLink util jumps 40% -> 95%
  t=18ms: first NCCL allreduce starts waiting on missing data; op latency balloons x3
  t=26ms: DMA completes, NCCL resumes, overall request latency experiences a 320ms tail in the run

- After HTS (windowed inflight cap):
  t=0ms: 16 replicas receive requests
  t=2ms: HTS allows 4 replicas to prefetch, others queued
  t=10ms: first batch completes, next batch begins; NVLink util peaks to 55% only; NCCL op times remain compact.

End of doc.
